intro: Planning to take down a tree in Burlington? The first question is not who you hire. It is whether the city will let you touch the tree at all. A Burlington tree removal permit is required for most mature private trees inside the urban boundary, and the rule that decides it is trunk size, not how the tree looks. Here is the honest version. The 20 cm rule, the urban-boundary catch that quietly exempts part of the city, the fee, the replacement-tree math, and the part most homeowners miss. Plenty of the time you do not need a removal at all. The right pruning, or one heavy limb off, fixes the problem and keeps you onside with the bylaw. We run an owner-led shop that does pruning and limb removal across south Ontario, so that is the lens we read these rules through. We are not lawyers, bylaws change, and we confirm the current rule for your specific tree before any cut. But this is the map.

sections.heading: When you actually need a permit in Burlington
paragraphs: Burlington protects private trees under its Private Tree By-law (By-law 040-2022), in effect since April 2022. The trigger is size. Any privately owned tree measuring 20 cm or more across the trunk (about 8 inches), measured at 1.37 m off the ground, needs a permit before it comes down.

That 20 cm line sits right in the middle of the western GTA. Toronto's rule only starts at 30 cm, while Oakville and Mississauga both catch trees at 15 cm. Burlington lands between them. So do not carry a number across a municipal line. A tree that is fair game in one town can be protected the moment you cross into the next.

Want to check your own tree before you call anyone? Wrap a tape measure around the trunk at chest height, then divide that number by about 3.14. That is your diameter. If it lands anywhere near 20 cm, treat it as protected until the city tells you otherwise.

• Permit needed: any private tree 20 cm or more across the trunk, inside Burlington's urban boundary.
  • Usually no permit: a tree under 20 cm across, measured at 1.37 m up the trunk (still worth confirming).
  • Protected at any size: heritage trees and endangered, threatened, or at-risk species.

sections.heading: The urban-boundary catch most guides skip
paragraphs: Here is the Burlington wrinkle the other GTA bylaws do not have. The Private Tree By-law only applies inside the city's urban boundary. Burlington is a large municipality, and a real chunk of it sits north of that line in rural and Greenbelt land, up around Lowville, Kilbride, and the escarpment.

If your property is outside the urban boundary, the city's private-tree permit does not govern your backyard trees the same way. That does not mean anything goes. Other rules can still apply: conservation authority regulations near valleys and the escarpment, woodland rules at the Region of Halton level, and species-at-risk protections. The point is that the city tree permit is not automatically the rule for your tree.

Quick check before you assume: a Burlington address alone does not tell you which side of the line you are on. Lots near the QEW and the lake are clearly urban. Properties up near the escarpment often are not. When the boundary is in question, we confirm it against the city map before reading you the bylaw, because the wrong assumption here changes the whole answer.

sections.heading: What the permit costs you, in money and in time
paragraphs: The application itself is cheap. The tree permit application processing fee is $54 plus HST, per application. That part rarely scares anyone off.
The replacement obligation is where it adds up. Burlington uses a size-based compensation ratio. The bigger the tree you remove, the more trees you owe back:

• 20 to 35 cm trunk: 2 replacement trees for every 1 removed.
  • 36 to 74 cm trunk: 3 replacement trees for every 1 removed.
  • 75 cm and up: 4 replacement trees for every 1 removed.

Take down one mature 80 cm maple and the city can ask for four trees back, or cash in lieu where there is no room to plant them. That is the real cost of a removal in Burlington, and it is the strongest argument for asking whether you need one at all.

Time is the other cost. The city has been working through high volumes of tree permit requests, so this is not a same-week approval. Budget several weeks from application to decision, and longer through the busy spring stretch. If a closing or a build depends on the work, plan the wait into your timeline rather than against it.

sections.heading: What happens if you skip it
paragraphs: Removing a protected tree without a permit is an offence under By-law 040-2022. Burlington enforces it through its administrative penalty system, so a quiet weekend removal can turn into a penalty per tree plus an order to replant what you took down.

The bigger exposure is the replacement order. The city can require the same 2 to 1, 3 to 1, or 4 to 1 trees back after the fact, on a tree you have already removed, with no say from you on where they go. Skipping the permit does not skip the replanting. It just removes your input on it.

Most homeowners miss this: a neighbour complaint is the usual trigger. Tree work is loud and visible. By the time a chipper is running in the driveway, everyone nearby knows a tree came down, and a protected-tree removal in plain sight is an easy call for someone to make.

sections.heading: The part most homeowners miss: you might not need a removal at all
paragraphs: Here is what the search hides. People look up the Burlington tree removal permit because they have a problem they want gone. A limb over the roof. Mess on the deck. Roots lifting the patio. Too much shade on the garden.
Removal is the biggest, slowest, most regulated answer to all of those. Often it is the wrong one.

Pruning is not a removal. Cutting back, thinning, or shaping a tree you are keeping does not trigger the removal permit at all. Burlington's own bylaw lets you prune up to a third of a tree's live crown without a permit. A good prune fixes most "this tree is a problem" complaints without the permit, the fee, or the replacement obligation. One bad branch is a limb removal, not a tree removal.

A real example of how this plays out: a homeowner calls about a big silver maple shading the whole backyard and dropping seeds everywhere, sure it has to go. Nine times out of ten the fix is a crown thin and a couple of low limbs off. Light comes through, the mess stops, no permit, no replacement trees owed. The tree stays and the bill is a fraction of a removal plus four replanted trees. And if a prune is the route you take, timing still matters for how cleanly the tree heals, which our guide on when to prune trees in southern Ontario walks through.

Sometimes removal really is the answer. A dead tree, a failing trunk, a species planted in the wrong spot. When that is the case you need the permit, and we will tell you so plainly rather than talk you into a prune that will not hold.

faqs.a: Usually yes, if it is a mature tree inside the urban boundary. Burlington's Private Tree By-law (040-2022) protects any private tree 20 cm or more in diameter, measured at 1.37 m up the trunk. Smaller trees are generally exempt, and properties outside the urban boundary are not covered the same way. Measure at chest height before you assume.

faqs.q: How much does a Burlington tree removal permit cost?
faqs.a: The application processing fee is $54 plus HST per application. The larger cost is replacement: Burlington requires 2 trees back for a 20 to 35 cm removal, 3 for 36 to 74 cm, and 4 for anything 75 cm and over, or cash in lieu where there is no room to plant. Fees change, so confirm the current figure with the city before you budget.

faqs.q: Does the Burlington tree bylaw apply everywhere in the city?
faqs.a: No. The Private Tree By-law only applies inside Burlington's urban boundary. A large rural and Greenbelt area to the north, near Lowville, Kilbride, and the escarpment, sits outside it. Other rules can still apply there, like conservation authority and woodland regulations, so outside the boundary does not mean no rules. Confirm which side of the line you are on first.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to prune a tree in Burlington?
faqs.a: No. The permit is for removing or injuring a protected tree. Burlington's bylaw lets you prune up to a third of a tree's live crown without a permit, and pruning a tree you are keeping does not trigger the removal permit at all. It is often the cheapest fix for a problem tree. Get in touch and we will tell you whether a prune solves it.

faqs.q: What if the tree is dead or dangerous?
faqs.a: Dead trees, trees with a terminal condition, and high-risk trees are exempt from the Burlington permit. For an immediate hazard, contact the city directly. We handle hazardous limbs by appointment, and we never touch anything on or near a hydro line, that is the utility's job.

On a big mature tree that can mean several new trees on your lot, so factor that in before you commit to a removal.

Worth knowing: the 30 cm threshold has been under review, with proposals to protect smaller trees. The safe move is to measure your tree and assume anything close to 30 cm across is protected until the city tells you otherwise. A Toronto tree removal permit is not a formality you can skip on a guess about your tree's size. And if your lot sits near a municipal line, the number changes the moment you cross it. Both Oakville and Mississauga protect trees at 15 cm, half of Toronto's threshold, so a tree that is fair game on one side of the border can be fully protected on the other. Burlington sits between, protecting trees at 20 cm.

sections.heading: What the permit costs you, in money and in time
paragraphs: There are two costs here, and both sit on top of the tree work itself. There is the city application fee, and there is the arborist report that has to go with the application. Neither is huge on its own, but they are real and they are separate line items.
Then there is time. Budget several weeks. The roughly 30 business day review is the floor, not a promise, and it stretches in busy season or if the city comes back asking for more detail.

One exception worth knowing: if a tree is an immediate hazard, there is a faster path. The city treats actively dangerous trees differently from a routine removal. That is the exception, not the everyday rule, so do not count on it for a tree that is simply in the way.

This is why timing matters. If you already know a tree needs attention, start early rather than the week you want the work done. And if the job turns out to be pruning rather than removal, our guide on when to prune trees in southern Ontario walks through the seasonal timing.

sections.heading: What happens if you skip it
paragraphs: The fines are the part people underestimate. Under Chapter 813, the penalty for removing or injuring a protected tree without a permit starts at $500 per tree and can run up to $100,000 per tree.
Read that again: per tree. Two trees, double the exposure. And the city does act on complaints. Neighbours notice when a mature tree disappears over a weekend, and they report it.

So the math is simple. A removal you could have permitted for a modest fee turns into a five-figure problem the moment you cut without one. It is not a gamble worth taking, and no honest contractor will tell you otherwise.

sections.heading: Where the rules get stricter: ravines, heritage, and city trees
paragraphs: Three situations tighten things beyond the standard private-tree rule:

• Ravine and natural-feature land. If your property sits in or near a protected ravine, a separate set of rules applies on top of the tree bylaw. The protections there are stronger.
  • City-owned trees. The tree on the boulevard or right at the curb is often the city's, not yours. You cannot touch it, and neither can we. That is city forestry's call.
  • Heritage properties and some development sites carry extra conditions of their own.

When you are unsure who owns the tree, or which set of rules stacks on top of which, that is a question to settle before anyone climbs. Guessing wrong on a ravine lot or a city tree is exactly how a small job becomes a fine.

sections.heading: The part most homeowners miss: you might not need a removal at all
paragraphs: Here is what we see on a lot of quote visits. The homeowner is braced for a full removal, and the permit headache that comes with it, and the actual problem is one limb hanging over the roof, or a canopy that has gotten too dense and heavy on one side.

Pruning a protected tree the right way, within the bylaw, often solves the problem with no removal permit at all. A healthy mature tree is an asset the city is trying to keep for good reasons, and keeping it, well pruned, is usually cheaper and faster than taking it down.

Worth asking before you commit to a removal: is the whole tree the problem, or is it a couple of limbs? More often than not, it is the limbs. That is exactly the work we do, whether it is careful pruning to bring a canopy back into shape or taking down a single heavy limb that is the real hazard.

One honest caveat: heavy pruning of a protected tree can still trigger the bylaw, because the rule covers injuring a tree, not only removing it. So the same check-first discipline applies. We confirm whether your specific job needs a permit before we touch the tree.

sections.heading: How we handle protected trees on a job
paragraphs: Our lane is pruning and limb removal, owner-led, across south Ontario. Full tree takedowns are not something we offer yet, so if your tree genuinely has to come out, we will tell you straight and point you to the right process rather than pretend it is our job.
For the pruning and limb work we do, the routine is the same every time:

• We read the bylaw for your property first and tell you honestly whether the work needs a permit before anything starts.
  • We keep cuts clean and within what a protected tree can take, so the tree stays healthy and you stay compliant.
  • We do not touch limbs on or near hydro lines. That is the utility's territory, every time, no exceptions.

A Toronto tree removal permit sounds like a wall, and for a genuine removal it is a real process you should not shortcut. But for most of the pruning and limb work a homeowner actually needs, the smarter path is to keep the tree, prune it right, and skip the permit headache entirely. Tell us what is going on with your tree and we will tell you which path you are on.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to remove a tree on my own property in Toronto?
faqs.a: Usually yes, if the tree is protected. Toronto's Private Tree By-law (Municipal Code Chapter 813) protects privately owned trees measuring 30 cm or more in diameter at 1.4 m up the trunk. Removing or seriously injuring one without a permit can bring fines from $500 to $100,000 per tree. Smaller trees may be exempt, but measure before you assume.

faqs.q: How big does a tree have to be before it is protected?
faqs.a: As of 2026 the threshold is 30 cm in diameter, measured at 1.4 m above the ground (DBH). The city has discussed lowering it, so anything close to that size should be treated as protected until you confirm the current rule for your property.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit just to prune a protected tree?
faqs.a: Sometimes. The bylaw covers injuring a tree, not only removing it, so heavy pruning of a protected tree can require a permit, while routine, careful pruning generally does not. We confirm whether your specific job crosses that line before we start any cut.

faqs.q: What happens if I remove a tree without a permit?
faqs.a: Under Chapter 813 the penalty starts at $500 per tree and can reach $100,000 per tree. The city acts on complaints, and neighbours do report unpermitted removals. A permit you could have obtained for a modest fee is far cheaper than the fine.

faqs.q: Do you handle the removal and the permit for me?
faqs.a: We focus on pruning and limb removal, not full tree takedowns, so we do not file removal permits. What we do is tell you honestly whether your job needs one, handle the pruning or limb work within the bylaw, and point you to the city's process if the tree genuinely has to come out.

title: When to Prune Oak Trees in Ontario · Tarzan Trimming
h1: When to Prune Oak Trees in Ontario (and Why the Calendar Matters More Than the Cut)
description: When to prune oak trees in Ontario: never April to October, because of oak wilt. Prune in the dormant season, November on. Here is the safe window.
focusKeyword: when to prune oak trees in Ontario
ctaHeading: Have an oak that needs pruning this winter?
ctaCopy: Send a photo of the tree and your address through the contact page. We will tell you whether it is a dormant-season job, whether any limb is urgent enough to look at sooner, and what the work involves. No deposit, no pressure.
intro: If you own an oak, the question of when to prune oak trees in Ontario is not a small scheduling detail. Get the timing wrong and you can open the door to oak wilt, a fungal disease that can kill a healthy red oak in a matter of weeks. The short version: do not prune your oaks between April and October. Wait for the dormant season. Here is the full picture, and why the month you cut matters more than how you cut.

sections.heading: The short answer: prune oaks in the dormant season
paragraphs: The safe window to prune an oak in Ontario runs from November through March, when the sap beetles that carry oak wilt are dormant and the tree is no longer pushing active growth.

The window to avoid is April through October. That is the warm stretch when those beetles are out, the tree is bleeding sap, and a fresh cut becomes a target. The Invasive Species Centre draws the line in the same place: no oak pruning until November.
So the rule is easy to remember. Cold and bare? Go ahead. Warm and leafy? Leave the saw in the truck unless the limb is a genuine hazard.

sections.heading: What oak wilt is, and why it rewrites the rules for oaks
paragraphs: Oak wilt is an invasive vascular disease caused by a fungus, Bretziella fagacearum. It clogs the vessels that move water and nutrients through the tree, so an infected oak essentially dies of thirst from the inside.
Red oaks are the most vulnerable. Once infected, a red oak can be dead in two to six weeks. White oaks tend to hang on longer, but they are not immune.

The disease moves two ways. Sap beetles pick up fungal spores and carry them to fresh wounds on other trees. And where oaks grow close together, their roots fuse underground, so the fungus can creep from a sick tree straight into the healthy one beside it.

sections.heading: Which oaks are most at risk in southern Ontario
paragraphs: Not every oak carries the same risk, so it helps to know what is in your yard. Oaks split into two broad camps, and the difference is more than academic once oak wilt is in the picture.

The red oak group covers red oak, black oak, and pin oak. You can usually spot them by leaves with pointed, bristle-tipped lobes. These are the high-casualty trees, the ones that can go from healthy to dead in a single summer.
The white oak group covers white oak, bur oak, and swamp white oak, with rounded, bristle-free leaf lobes. They resist the disease better and decline more slowly. Better is not the same as safe.
If you are not sure which one you have, do not stress about it. The dormant-season rule is the right habit for any oak, and it costs you nothing to apply it across the board.

sections.heading: Why a fresh pruning cut is the part you control
paragraphs: Most homeowners cannot do much about root grafts between mature oaks. What you can control is whether you hand the beetles an open wound during their active season.

A pruning cut in July smells like dinner. The sap weeps, the beetles follow the scent, and they show up carrying spores from wherever they fed last. Make that same cut in January and the beetles are grounded, the sap is not running, and the tree has time to wall the wound off before spring.

Quick note if you already slipped up: if you had to prune an oak between April and October, seal the wound right away. A thin coat of pruning paint or shellac over the cut is one of the few times wound dressing is genuinely recommended, precisely because it hides the fresh sap from the beetles.

sections.heading: Oak wilt is now in Ontario, and that is recent news
paragraphs: For years this was a problem Ontario watched from across the border. That changed in 2023, when oak wilt was confirmed in Canada for the first time on a residential property in Niagara Falls. Detections followed in Niagara-on-the-Lake and the Township of Springwater.

It is already established in two dozen U.S. states that border Canada, so the pressure is not letting up. That is the reason arborists across southern Ontario have tightened up on oak-pruning timing in the last couple of seasons. It stopped being theoretical.

If you think you are looking at an infected oak, with leaves browning from the top down and dropping in mid-summer, the Canadian Food Inspection Agency is the body to report it to. Do not move the wood off the property.

sections.heading: When a branch genuinely cannot wait
paragraphs: Timing rules bend for safety. If a storm cracks an oak limb over your driveway in July, you do not leave it hanging for four months because the calendar says so. A broken limb is already an open wound and a falling hazard, and the hazard wins.

In that case the order is simple: deal with the danger, then protect the tree. Remove or make safe the broken limb, and seal the cut surface the same day to keep the beetles off it. That is the narrow exception, not the everyday rule.

Hanging, split, or storm-damaged oak limbs are exactly the kind of work covered under our limb removal service. If a limb is over a roof, a walkway, or a hydro line, say so when you reach out so we can look at it sooner rather than later.

sections.heading: What good oak pruning actually involves
paragraphs: When the dormant season comes around, good oak pruning is mostly about restraint. A healthy mature oak rarely needs much taken off in a single year.
Deadwood and damage first. Dead, broken, and rubbing branches are the priority. They are doing the tree no good, and a few of them are a hazard waiting for a windy night.

A light touch on live wood. Stripping too much green growth at once stresses the tree and forces a flush of weak, crowded regrowth. The sensible habit is to leave the bulk of the live canopy alone in any given winter.

Clean cuts at the collar. Cuts made just outside the branch collar, not flush against the trunk, let the tree seal itself properly. That sealing response is the whole reason dormant-season timing works in the first place.
If that sounds like more judgment than you want to be making from the ground with a pole saw, that is exactly the kind of call worth handing to someone who does it for a living.

sections.heading: A simple oak-pruning calendar for southern Ontario
paragraphs: If you remember nothing else about when to prune oak trees in Ontario, remember this calendar.
November to March: prune freely. This is your window for shaping, deadwood removal, and clearance cuts. Line it up now and the work lands in the right season.
April to October: hands off, unless a limb is a safety hazard. If you have no choice but to cut, seal the wound the same day.

Other species have their own timing, and most south-Ontario trees are more forgiving than oaks. Our guide to when to prune trees in southern Ontario walks through the rest of them. For the oak itself, the dormant-season rule is the one worth being strict about.

Getting the timing right on when to prune oak trees in Ontario really comes down to staying patient through the warm months and being organized for winter. If you have an oak you want shaped or cleaned up, the smart move is to book the tree pruning work now so it happens in the dormant window, across the communities we cover in south Ontario.

faqs.q: When is it safe to prune oak trees in Ontario?
faqs.a: From November through March, during the dormant season. That is when the sap beetles that spread oak wilt are inactive and a fresh cut is far less likely to attract them. The Invasive Species Centre recommends no oak pruning until November.

faqs.q: Why can't I prune oak trees in summer?
faqs.a: Because April through October is when sap beetles are active. A fresh summer pruning cut weeps sap, attracts those beetles, and they can deliver oak wilt spores straight into the open wound. The same cut made in winter carries almost none of that risk.

faqs.q: Is oak wilt actually present in Ontario?
faqs.a: Yes. It was confirmed in Canada for the first time in 2023 on a residential property in Niagara Falls, with further detections in Niagara-on-the-Lake and the Township of Springwater. It is also established in many U.S. states along the border, which is why timing matters here now.

faqs.q: What should I do if a storm breaks an oak limb in July?
faqs.a: Safety comes first. A broken or hanging limb is already a wound and a hazard, so it gets dealt with regardless of season. Make the limb safe, then seal the cut surface the same day with pruning paint or shellac to keep beetles away from the fresh wood.

faqs.q: Do all oak trees get oak wilt?
faqs.a: All oaks can be affected, but red oaks are by far the most vulnerable and can die within two to six weeks of infection. White oaks are more resistant and tend to decline more slowly. Either way, the dormant-season pruning rule is the safe habit for any oak.
